case_info.scenario: An 11-year-old boy with a history of cleft palate repair, placement of multiple sets of pressure-equalizing tubes, and suspected ectodermal dysplasia (not confirmed with genetic testing) was referred from a general ear, nose, and throat physician. The patient had presented with a chief concern of a 1-year history of hearing loss. He had no otorrhea or otalgia during this time. Otoscopic examination of the ear showed bilateral dead-end ear canals with smooth hypervascular fibrosis extending medially from the bony cartilaginous junction. There were no granulation tissue, pit, or tract. Computed tomography (CT) imaging showed bilateral severe external auditory canal (EAC) stenosis due to heterotopic ossification in the medial aspects of each EAC and nonossified opacification extending to the tympanic membrane (Figure). The middle and inner ears were otherwise normal. Noncontrast magnetic resonance imaging showed bilateral EAC stenosis with soft tissue, and on diffusion-weighted imaging the material within the EAC did not show decreased diffusivity. Behavioral pure-tone audiometry revealed bilateral moderately severe mixed hearing loss. Speech perception was greater than 95% bilaterally, and tympanometry was flat bilaterally. The patient’s mother indicated that she has had a similar set of symptoms for much of her life. She reported maximum conductive hearing loss for which she had not had hearing rehabilitation nor further workup. Otoscopic examination of the mother’s ears showed identical findings to the patient.
case_info.caption: Computed tomography (CT) imaging showing heterotopic ossification within the external auditory canals (yellow arrowheads) and opacification (asterisks) extending to the mineralized tympanic membranes (blue arrowheads).
case_info.explanation: The ectodermal dysplasia syndromes are a group of rare genetic diseases that occur when there is a congenital defect in at least 2 ectodermal derivatives, one of which involves the hair, teeth, nails, or sweat glands. The inheritance pattern is variable (typically X-linked recessive or autosomal dominant) depending on the specific syndrome, and the estimated incidence is 0.7 to 1 per 100 000 live births.1,2Patients with ectodermal dysplasia typically have ear-, nose-, and throat-related disease manifestations, such as nasal obstruction/dryness, otitis media, and hearing loss.2 Conductive hearing loss is relatively common and can result from obstruction of the EACs; however, all listed possible diagnoses represent rare etiologies of conductive hearing loss.3,4The physical examination finding of dead-end ear canals could be caused by any of the diagnoses, although aural atresia is a congenital condition that would have been present throughout the life of the patient and prevented prior ear tube placement; furthermore, aural atresia is often accompanied by microtia of the pinna. The presence of bilateral disease makes ear canal cholesteatoma less likely, as does the young age of the patient.4Diagnostic features in this case also include CT findings showing ear canals filled with debris of mineralized/ossified material, but without EAC enlargement/erosion, as expected in keratosis obturans. Ear canal cholesteatoma typically occurs in older children or adults and results in asymmetric bone erosion with drainage. Noncontrast magnetic resonance imaging with diffusion-weighted imaging can also be used to help exclude alternative diagnoses, including cholesteatoma, which classically demonstrates decreased diffusivity. Diagnosis was made for this patient from his examination and imaging findings in the setting of ectodermal dysplasia. The presence of the same finding in the patient’s mother supports a hereditary origin rather than a spontaneous genetic mutation or other sporadic cause. Ectoderm plays a critical role in normal ear development, including external, middle, and inner ear structures, and otologic manifestations of ectodermal dysplasia, reported in small case series, include varied manifestations of disease, such as chronic otitis media, sensorineural hearing loss, cerumen impaction, and pinna abnormalities.1,5-7There have been few reported cases of external ear canal stenosis due to ectodermal dysplasia, and there are no descriptions of physical examination findings.1,7,8One patient with EAC stenosis due recurrent otitis externa underwent CT, which showed bilateral soft tissue opacification filling the EACs.8 Management of ectodermal dysplasia requires a multidisciplinary team, and treatment is typically aimed toward symptom management. It is recommended that patients with ectodermal dysplasia of any age undergo hearing tests if hearing loss is suspected. Treatment of common otologic manifestations includes placement of ear tubes for recurrent acute or chronic serous otitis media, use of hearing aids for sensorineural hearing loss, and lubricant ear drops to help soften ear wax. In this case, canaloplasty and bone-conduction hearing aid devices were discussed with the patient and his family. Due to concerns that the ear canal fibrosis would recur given his underlying condition, it was recommended that the patient pursue a bone-anchored hearing aid. The patient started with a trial of a soft-band bone conduction device and ultimately underwent surgery for placement of a transcutaneous active bone conduction implant. Due to his ectodermal dysplasia, placement of a percutaneous device was not recommended. The patient’s mother expressed interest in understanding her options for treatment as well. To our knowledge, this case demonstrates the first reported description of otoscopic findings in a family with ear canal stenosis due to ectodermal dysplasia and describes characteristic CT findings. Ectodermal dysplasia can cause EAC stenosis that manifests in childhood, and all patients with ectodermal dysplasia should undergo otologic and audiologic assessment.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,

* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: The ectodermal dysplasia syndromes are a group of rare genetic diseases that occur when there is a congenital defect in at least 2 ectodermal derivatives, one of which involves the hair, teeth, nails, or sweat glands. The inheritance pattern is variable (typically X-linked recessive or autosomal dominant) depending on the specific syndrome, and the estimated incidence is 0.7 to 1 per 100 000 live births.1,2Patients with ectodermal dysplasia typically have ear-, nose-, and throat-related disease manifestations, such as nasal obstruction/dryness, otitis media, and hearing loss.2 Conductive hearing loss is relatively common and can result from obstruction of the EACs; however, all listed possible diagnoses represent rare etiologies of conductive hearing loss.3,4The physical examination finding of dead-end ear canals could be caused by any of the diagnoses, although aural atresia is a congenital condition that would have been present throughout the life of the patient and prevented prior ear tube placement; furthermore, aural atresia is often accompanied by microtia of the pinna. The presence of bilateral disease makes ear canal cholesteatoma less likely, as does the young age of the patient.4Diagnostic features in this case also include CT findings showing ear canals filled with debris of mineralized/ossified material, but without EAC enlargement/erosion, as expected in keratosis obturans. Ear canal cholesteatoma typically occurs in older children or adults and results in asymmetric bone erosion with drainage. Noncontrast magnetic resonance imaging with diffusion-weighted imaging can also be used to help exclude alternative diagnoses, including cholesteatoma, which classically demonstrates decreased diffusivity. Diagnosis was made for this patient from his examination and imaging findings in the setting of ectodermal dysplasia. The presence of the same finding in the patient’s mother supports a hereditary origin rather than a spontaneous genetic mutation or other sporadic cause. Ectoderm plays a critical role in normal ear development, including external, middle, and inner ear structures, and otologic manifestations of ectodermal dysplasia, reported in small case series, include varied manifestations of disease, such as chronic otitis media, sensorineural hearing loss, cerumen impaction, and pinna abnormalities.1,5-7There have been few reported cases of external ear canal stenosis due to ectodermal dysplasia, and there are no descriptions of physical examination findings.1,7,8One patient with EAC stenosis due recurrent otitis externa underwent CT, which showed bilateral soft tissue opacification filling the EACs.8 Management of ectodermal dysplasia requires a multidisciplinary team, and treatment is typically aimed toward symptom management. It is recommended that patients with ectodermal dysplasia of any age undergo hearing tests if hearing loss is suspected. Treatment of common otologic manifestations includes placement of ear tubes for recurrent acute or chronic serous otitis media, use of hearing aids for sensorineural hearing loss, and lubricant ear drops to help soften ear wax. In this case, canaloplasty and bone-conduction hearing aid devices were discussed with the patient and his family. Due to concerns that the ear canal fibrosis would recur given his underlying condition, it was recommended that the patient pursue a bone-anchored hearing aid. The patient started with a trial of a soft-band bone conduction device and ultimately underwent surgery for placement of a transcutaneous active bone conduction implant. Due to his ectodermal dysplasia, placement of a percutaneous device was not recommended. The patient’s mother expressed interest in understanding her options for treatment as well. To our knowledge, this case demonstrates the first reported description of otoscopic findings in a family with ear canal stenosis due to ectodermal dysplasia and describes characteristic CT findings. Ectodermal dysplasia can cause EAC stenosis that manifests in childhood, and all patients with ectodermal dysplasia should undergo otologic and audiologic assessment.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

case_info.explanation: The ectodermal dysplasia syndromes are a group of rare genetic diseases that occur when there is a congenital defect in at least 2 ectodermal derivatives, one of which involves the hair, teeth, nails, or sweat glands. The inheritance pattern is variable (typically X-linked recessive or autosomal dominant) depending on the specific syndrome, and the estimated incidence is 0.7 to 1 per 100 000 live births.1,2Patients with ectodermal dysplasia typically have ear-, nose-, and throat-related disease manifestations, such as nasal obstruction/dryness, otitis media, and hearing loss.2 Conductive hearing loss is relatively common and can result from obstruction of the EACs; however, all listed possible diagnoses represent rare etiologies of conductive hearing loss.3,4The physical examination finding of dead-end ear canals could be caused by any of the diagnoses, although aural atresia is a congenital condition that would have been present throughout the life of the patient and prevented prior ear tube placement; furthermore, aural atresia is often accompanied by microtia of the pinna. The presence of bilateral disease makes ear canal cholesteatoma less likely, as does the young age of the patient.4Diagnostic features in this case also include CT findings showing ear canals filled with debris of mineralized/ossified material, but without EAC enlargement/erosion, as expected in keratosis obturans. Ear canal cholesteatoma typically occurs in older children or adults and results in asymmetric bone erosion with drainage. Noncontrast magnetic resonance imaging with diffusion-weighted imaging can also be used to help exclude alternative diagnoses, including cholesteatoma, which classically demonstrates decreased diffusivity. Diagnosis was made for this patient from his examination and imaging findings in the setting of ectodermal dysplasia. The presence of the same finding in the patient’s mother supports a hereditary origin rather than a spontaneous genetic mutation or other sporadic cause. Ectoderm plays a critical role in normal ear development, including external, middle, and inner ear structures, and otologic manifestations of ectodermal dysplasia, reported in small case series, include varied manifestations of disease, such as chronic otitis media, sensorineural hearing loss, cerumen impaction, and pinna abnormalities.1,5-7There have been few reported cases of external ear canal stenosis due to ectodermal dysplasia, and there are no descriptions of physical examination findings.1,7,8One patient with EAC stenosis due recurrent otitis externa underwent CT, which showed bilateral soft tissue opacification filling the EACs.8 Management of ectodermal dysplasia requires a multidisciplinary team, and treatment is typically aimed toward symptom management. It is recommended that patients with ectodermal dysplasia of any age undergo hearing tests if hearing loss is suspected. Treatment of common otologic manifestations includes placement of ear tubes for recurrent acute or chronic serous otitis media, use of hearing aids for sensorineural hearing loss, and lubricant ear drops to help soften ear wax. In this case, canaloplasty and bone-conduction hearing aid devices were discussed with the patient and his family. Due to concerns that the ear canal fibrosis would recur given his underlying condition, it was recommended that the patient pursue a bone-anchored hearing aid. The patient started with a trial of a soft-band bone conduction device and ultimately underwent surgery for placement of a transcutaneous active bone conduction implant. Due to his ectodermal dysplasia, placement of a percutaneous device was not recommended. The patient’s mother expressed interest in understanding her options for treatment as well. To our knowledge, this case demonstrates the first reported description of otoscopic findings in a family with ear canal stenosis due to ectodermal dysplasia and describes characteristic CT findings. Ectodermal dysplasia can cause EAC stenosis that manifests in childhood, and all patients with ectodermal dysplasia should undergo otologic and audiologic assessment.

case_info.caption: Computed tomography (CT) imaging showing heterotopic ossification within the external auditory canals (yellow arrowheads) and opacification (asterisks) extending to the mineralized tympanic membranes (blue arrowheads).
case_info.explanation: The ectodermal dysplasia syndromes are a group of rare genetic diseases that occur when there is a congenital defect in at least 2 ectodermal derivatives, one of which involves the hair, teeth, nails, or sweat glands. The inheritance pattern is variable (typically X-linked recessive or autosomal dominant) depending on the specific syndrome, and the estimated incidence is 0.7 to 1 per 100 000 live births.1,2Patients with ectodermal dysplasia typically have ear-, nose-, and throat-related disease manifestations, such as nasal obstruction/dryness, otitis media, and hearing loss.2 Conductive hearing loss is relatively common and can result from obstruction of the EACs; however, all listed possible diagnoses represent rare etiologies of conductive hearing loss.3,4The physical examination finding of dead-end ear canals could be caused by any of the diagnoses, although aural atresia is a congenital condition that would have been present throughout the life of the patient and prevented prior ear tube placement; furthermore, aural atresia is often accompanied by microtia of the pinna. The presence of bilateral disease makes ear canal cholesteatoma less likely, as does the young age of the patient.4Diagnostic features in this case also include CT findings showing ear canals filled with debris of mineralized/ossified material, but without EAC enlargement/erosion, as expected in keratosis obturans. Ear canal cholesteatoma typically occurs in older children or adults and results in asymmetric bone erosion with drainage. Noncontrast magnetic resonance imaging with diffusion-weighted imaging can also be used to help exclude alternative diagnoses, including cholesteatoma, which classically demonstrates decreased diffusivity. Diagnosis was made for this patient from his examination and imaging findings in the setting of ectodermal dysplasia. The presence of the same finding in the patient’s mother supports a hereditary origin rather than a spontaneous genetic mutation or other sporadic cause. Ectoderm plays a critical role in normal ear development, including external, middle, and inner ear structures, and otologic manifestations of ectodermal dysplasia, reported in small case series, include varied manifestations of disease, such as chronic otitis media, sensorineural hearing loss, cerumen impaction, and pinna abnormalities.1,5-7There have been few reported cases of external ear canal stenosis due to ectodermal dysplasia, and there are no descriptions of physical examination findings.1,7,8One patient with EAC stenosis due recurrent otitis externa underwent CT, which showed bilateral soft tissue opacification filling the EACs.8 Management of ectodermal dysplasia requires a multidisciplinary team, and treatment is typically aimed toward symptom management. It is recommended that patients with ectodermal dysplasia of any age undergo hearing tests if hearing loss is suspected. Treatment of common otologic manifestations includes placement of ear tubes for recurrent acute or chronic serous otitis media, use of hearing aids for sensorineural hearing loss, and lubricant ear drops to help soften ear wax. In this case, canaloplasty and bone-conduction hearing aid devices were discussed with the patient and his family. Due to concerns that the ear canal fibrosis would recur given his underlying condition, it was recommended that the patient pursue a bone-anchored hearing aid. The patient started with a trial of a soft-band bone conduction device and ultimately underwent surgery for placement of a transcutaneous active bone conduction implant. Due to his ectodermal dysplasia, placement of a percutaneous device was not recommended. The patient’s mother expressed interest in understanding her options for treatment as well. To our knowledge, this case demonstrates the first reported description of otoscopic findings in a family with ear canal stenosis due to ectodermal dysplasia and describes characteristic CT findings. Ectodermal dysplasia can cause EAC stenosis that manifests in childhood, and all patients with ectodermal dysplasia should undergo otologic and audiologic assessment.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
An 11-year-old boy with a history of cleft palate repair, placement of multiple sets of pressure-equalizing tubes, and suspected ectodermal dysplasia (not confirmed with genetic testing) was referred from a general ear, nose, and throat physician. The patient had presented with a chief concern of a 1-year history of hearing loss. He had no otorrhea or otalgia during this time. Otoscopic examination of the ear showed bilateral dead-end ear canals with smooth hypervascular fibrosis extending medially from the bony cartilaginous junction. There were no granulation tissue, pit, or tract. Computed tomography (CT) imaging showed bilateral severe external auditory canal (EAC) stenosis due to heterotopic ossification in the medial aspects of each EAC and nonossified opacification extending to the tympanic membrane (Figure). The middle and inner ears were otherwise normal. Noncontrast magnetic resonance imaging showed bilateral EAC stenosis with soft tissue, and on diffusion-weighted imaging the material within the EAC did not show decreased diffusivity. Behavioral pure-tone audiometry revealed bilateral moderately severe mixed hearing loss. Speech perception was greater than 95% bilaterally, and tympanometry was flat bilaterally. The patient’s mother indicated that she has had a similar set of symptoms for much of her life. She reported maximum conductive hearing loss for which she had not had hearing rehabilitation nor further workup. Otoscopic examination of the mother’s ears showed identical findings to the patient.

You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

   Definition:

   Scoring:

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."

       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,

       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

   Definition:

     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.

case_info.explanation: The ectodermal dysplasia syndromes are a group of rare genetic diseases that occur when there is a congenital defect in at least 2 ectodermal derivatives, one of which involves the hair, teeth, nails, or sweat glands. The inheritance pattern is variable (typically X-linked recessive or autosomal dominant) depending on the specific syndrome, and the estimated incidence is 0.7 to 1 per 100 000 live births.1,2Patients with ectodermal dysplasia typically have ear-, nose-, and throat-related disease manifestations, such as nasal obstruction/dryness, otitis media, and hearing loss.2 Conductive hearing loss is relatively common and can result from obstruction of the EACs; however, all listed possible diagnoses represent rare etiologies of conductive hearing loss.3,4The physical examination finding of dead-end ear canals could be caused by any of the diagnoses, although aural atresia is a congenital condition that would have been present throughout the life of the patient and prevented prior ear tube placement; furthermore, aural atresia is often accompanied by microtia of the pinna. The presence of bilateral disease makes ear canal cholesteatoma less likely, as does the young age of the patient.4Diagnostic features in this case also include CT findings showing ear canals filled with debris of mineralized/ossified material, but without EAC enlargement/erosion, as expected in keratosis obturans. Ear canal cholesteatoma typically occurs in older children or adults and results in asymmetric bone erosion with drainage. Noncontrast magnetic resonance imaging with diffusion-weighted imaging can also be used to help exclude alternative diagnoses, including cholesteatoma, which classically demonstrates decreased diffusivity. Diagnosis was made for this patient from his examination and imaging findings in the setting of ectodermal dysplasia. The presence of the same finding in the patient’s mother supports a hereditary origin rather than a spontaneous genetic mutation or other sporadic cause. Ectoderm plays a critical role in normal ear development, including external, middle, and inner ear structures, and otologic manifestations of ectodermal dysplasia, reported in small case series, include varied manifestations of disease, such as chronic otitis media, sensorineural hearing loss, cerumen impaction, and pinna abnormalities.1,5-7There have been few reported cases of external ear canal stenosis due to ectodermal dysplasia, and there are no descriptions of physical examination findings.1,7,8One patient with EAC stenosis due recurrent otitis externa underwent CT, which showed bilateral soft tissue opacification filling the EACs.8 Management of ectodermal dysplasia requires a multidisciplinary team, and treatment is typically aimed toward symptom management. It is recommended that patients with ectodermal dysplasia of any age undergo hearing tests if hearing loss is suspected. Treatment of common otologic manifestations includes placement of ear tubes for recurrent acute or chronic serous otitis media, use of hearing aids for sensorineural hearing loss, and lubricant ear drops to help soften ear wax. In this case, canaloplasty and bone-conduction hearing aid devices were discussed with the patient and his family. Due to concerns that the ear canal fibrosis would recur given his underlying condition, it was recommended that the patient pursue a bone-anchored hearing aid. The patient started with a trial of a soft-band bone conduction device and ultimately underwent surgery for placement of a transcutaneous active bone conduction implant. Due to his ectodermal dysplasia, placement of a percutaneous device was not recommended. The patient’s mother expressed interest in understanding her options for treatment as well. To our knowledge, this case demonstrates the first reported description of otoscopic findings in a family with ear canal stenosis due to ectodermal dysplasia and describes characteristic CT findings. Ectodermal dysplasia can cause EAC stenosis that manifests in childhood, and all patients with ectodermal dysplasia should undergo otologic and audiologic assessment.

case_info.scenario: An 11-year-old boy with a history of cleft palate repair, placement of multiple sets of pressure-equalizing tubes, and suspected ectodermal dysplasia (not confirmed with genetic testing) was referred from a general ear, nose, and throat physician. The patient had presented with a chief concern of a 1-year history of hearing loss. He had no otorrhea or otalgia during this time. Otoscopic examination of the ear showed bilateral dead-end ear canals with smooth hypervascular fibrosis extending medially from the bony cartilaginous junction. There were no granulation tissue, pit, or tract. Computed tomography (CT) imaging showed bilateral severe external auditory canal (EAC) stenosis due to heterotopic ossification in the medial aspects of each EAC and nonossified opacification extending to the tympanic membrane (Figure). The middle and inner ears were otherwise normal. Noncontrast magnetic resonance imaging showed bilateral EAC stenosis with soft tissue, and on diffusion-weighted imaging the material within the EAC did not show decreased diffusivity. Behavioral pure-tone audiometry revealed bilateral moderately severe mixed hearing loss. Speech perception was greater than 95% bilaterally, and tympanometry was flat bilaterally. The patient’s mother indicated that she has had a similar set of symptoms for much of her life. She reported maximum conductive hearing loss for which she had not had hearing rehabilitation nor further workup. Otoscopic examination of the mother’s ears showed identical findings to the patient.
case_info.caption: Computed tomography (CT) imaging showing heterotopic ossification within the external auditory canals (yellow arrowheads) and opacification (asterisks) extending to the mineralized tympanic membranes (blue arrowheads).
case_info.explanation: The ectodermal dysplasia syndromes are a group of rare genetic diseases that occur when there is a congenital defect in at least 2 ectodermal derivatives, one of which involves the hair, teeth, nails, or sweat glands. The inheritance pattern is variable (typically X-linked recessive or autosomal dominant) depending on the specific syndrome, and the estimated incidence is 0.7 to 1 per 100 000 live births.1,2Patients with ectodermal dysplasia typically have ear-, nose-, and throat-related disease manifestations, such as nasal obstruction/dryness, otitis media, and hearing loss.2 Conductive hearing loss is relatively common and can result from obstruction of the EACs; however, all listed possible diagnoses represent rare etiologies of conductive hearing loss.3,4The physical examination finding of dead-end ear canals could be caused by any of the diagnoses, although aural atresia is a congenital condition that would have been present throughout the life of the patient and prevented prior ear tube placement; furthermore, aural atresia is often accompanied by microtia of the pinna. The presence of bilateral disease makes ear canal cholesteatoma less likely, as does the young age of the patient.4Diagnostic features in this case also include CT findings showing ear canals filled with debris of mineralized/ossified material, but without EAC enlargement/erosion, as expected in keratosis obturans. Ear canal cholesteatoma typically occurs in older children or adults and results in asymmetric bone erosion with drainage. Noncontrast magnetic resonance imaging with diffusion-weighted imaging can also be used to help exclude alternative diagnoses, including cholesteatoma, which classically demonstrates decreased diffusivity. Diagnosis was made for this patient from his examination and imaging findings in the setting of ectodermal dysplasia. The presence of the same finding in the patient’s mother supports a hereditary origin rather than a spontaneous genetic mutation or other sporadic cause. Ectoderm plays a critical role in normal ear development, including external, middle, and inner ear structures, and otologic manifestations of ectodermal dysplasia, reported in small case series, include varied manifestations of disease, such as chronic otitis media, sensorineural hearing loss, cerumen impaction, and pinna abnormalities.1,5-7There have been few reported cases of external ear canal stenosis due to ectodermal dysplasia, and there are no descriptions of physical examination findings.1,7,8One patient with EAC stenosis due recurrent otitis externa underwent CT, which showed bilateral soft tissue opacification filling the EACs.8 Management of ectodermal dysplasia requires a multidisciplinary team, and treatment is typically aimed toward symptom management. It is recommended that patients with ectodermal dysplasia of any age undergo hearing tests if hearing loss is suspected. Treatment of common otologic manifestations includes placement of ear tubes for recurrent acute or chronic serous otitis media, use of hearing aids for sensorineural hearing loss, and lubricant ear drops to help soften ear wax. In this case, canaloplasty and bone-conduction hearing aid devices were discussed with the patient and his family. Due to concerns that the ear canal fibrosis would recur given his underlying condition, it was recommended that the patient pursue a bone-anchored hearing aid. The patient started with a trial of a soft-band bone conduction device and ultimately underwent surgery for placement of a transcutaneous active bone conduction implant. Due to his ectodermal dysplasia, placement of a percutaneous device was not recommended. The patient’s mother expressed interest in understanding her options for treatment as well. To our knowledge, this case demonstrates the first reported description of otoscopic findings in a family with ear canal stenosis due to ectodermal dysplasia and describes characteristic CT findings. Ectodermal dysplasia can cause EAC stenosis that manifests in childhood, and all patients with ectodermal dysplasia should undergo otologic and audiologic assessment.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

case_info.caption: Computed tomography (CT) imaging showing heterotopic ossification within the external auditory canals (yellow arrowheads) and opacification (asterisks) extending to the mineralized tympanic membranes (blue arrowheads).
case_info.explanation: The ectodermal dysplasia syndromes are a group of rare genetic diseases that occur when there is a congenital defect in at least 2 ectodermal derivatives, one of which involves the hair, teeth, nails, or sweat glands. The inheritance pattern is variable (typically X-linked recessive or autosomal dominant) depending on the specific syndrome, and the estimated incidence is 0.7 to 1 per 100 000 live births.1,2Patients with ectodermal dysplasia typically have ear-, nose-, and throat-related disease manifestations, such as nasal obstruction/dryness, otitis media, and hearing loss.2 Conductive hearing loss is relatively common and can result from obstruction of the EACs; however, all listed possible diagnoses represent rare etiologies of conductive hearing loss.3,4The physical examination finding of dead-end ear canals could be caused by any of the diagnoses, although aural atresia is a congenital condition that would have been present throughout the life of the patient and prevented prior ear tube placement; furthermore, aural atresia is often accompanied by microtia of the pinna. The presence of bilateral disease makes ear canal cholesteatoma less likely, as does the young age of the patient.4Diagnostic features in this case also include CT findings showing ear canals filled with debris of mineralized/ossified material, but without EAC enlargement/erosion, as expected in keratosis obturans. Ear canal cholesteatoma typically occurs in older children or adults and results in asymmetric bone erosion with drainage. Noncontrast magnetic resonance imaging with diffusion-weighted imaging can also be used to help exclude alternative diagnoses, including cholesteatoma, which classically demonstrates decreased diffusivity. Diagnosis was made for this patient from his examination and imaging findings in the setting of ectodermal dysplasia. The presence of the same finding in the patient’s mother supports a hereditary origin rather than a spontaneous genetic mutation or other sporadic cause. Ectoderm plays a critical role in normal ear development, including external, middle, and inner ear structures, and otologic manifestations of ectodermal dysplasia, reported in small case series, include varied manifestations of disease, such as chronic otitis media, sensorineural hearing loss, cerumen impaction, and pinna abnormalities.1,5-7There have been few reported cases of external ear canal stenosis due to ectodermal dysplasia, and there are no descriptions of physical examination findings.1,7,8One patient with EAC stenosis due recurrent otitis externa underwent CT, which showed bilateral soft tissue opacification filling the EACs.8 Management of ectodermal dysplasia requires a multidisciplinary team, and treatment is typically aimed toward symptom management. It is recommended that patients with ectodermal dysplasia of any age undergo hearing tests if hearing loss is suspected. Treatment of common otologic manifestations includes placement of ear tubes for recurrent acute or chronic serous otitis media, use of hearing aids for sensorineural hearing loss, and lubricant ear drops to help soften ear wax. case_info.caption: Computed tomography (CT) imaging showing heterotopic ossification within the external auditory canals (yellow arrowheads) and opacification (asterisks) extending to the mineralized tympanic membranes (blue arrowheads).
case_info.explanation: The ectodermal dysplasia syndromes are a group of rare genetic diseases that occur when there is a congenital defect in at least 2 ectodermal derivatives, one of which involves the hair, teeth, nails, or sweat glands. The inheritance pattern is variable (typically X-linked recessive or autosomal dominant) depending on the specific syndrome, and the estimated incidence is 0.7 to 1 per 100 000 live births.1,2Patients with ectodermal dysplasia typically have ear-, nose-, and throat-related disease manifestations, such as nasal obstruction/dryness, otitis media, and hearing loss.2 Conductive hearing loss is relatively common and can result from obstruction of the EACs; however, all listed possible diagnoses represent rare etiologies of conductive hearing loss.3,4The physical examination finding of dead-end ear canals could be caused by any of the diagnoses, although aural atresia is a congenital condition that would have been present throughout the life of the patient and prevented prior ear tube placement; furthermore, aural atresia is often accompanied by microtia of the pinna. The presence of bilateral disease makes ear canal cholesteatoma less likely, as does the young age of the patient.4Diagnostic features in this case also include CT findings showing ear canals filled with debris of mineralized/ossified material, but without EAC enlargement/erosion, as expected in keratosis obturans. Ear canal cholesteatoma typically occurs in older children or adults and results in asymmetric bone erosion with drainage. Noncontrast magnetic resonance imaging with diffusion-weighted imaging can also be used to help exclude alternative diagnoses, including cholesteatoma, which classically demonstrates decreased diffusivity. Diagnosis was made for this patient from his examination and imaging findings in the setting of ectodermal dysplasia. The presence of the same finding in the patient’s mother supports a hereditary origin rather than a spontaneous genetic mutation or other sporadic cause.
